fields.before: The correct answer is ア: “a-Use the current one, b-Use the current one.” This question asks how identification codes should be handled when migrating without stopping the system, using the old and new methods together (parallel migration). The decisive clues are the two premises set out in the question. First, it has been decided that the file (table) for managing the lending history will continue to use the one from the current system as-is. Each lending history record points to which book was borrowed and which user borrowed it by means of the book identification number and the user number on the user card. If the numbers were renumbered into a new scheme along with the migration, the numbers in the history records already accumulated and the numbers in the records to be added from now on would become different things, and once mixed in the same table it would no longer be possible to trace the same book or the same user. One could also create a mapping table between old and new numbers and convert all past data at once, but that departs from the premise of using the current file as-is, and it invites the risk of conversion errors and of operations coming to a halt. Second, during the migration period the current barcodes and the newly introduced RFID are used together. Attaching RFID to several hundred thousand books cannot be finished all at once, so books that already have RFID and books that still have only a barcode will be mixed together for a long time. To make sure the same book is recognized no matter which medium is read, it is natural to make the identification number written into the RFID the same as the current identification number that the book’s barcode represents. The same applies to the user number: even when switching to new user cards with built-in RFID, if the user number is carried over unchanged, the user of an old card and the user of a new card are linked as the same person in the history, so operations can continue without worrying about the order in which cards are replaced. In addition, if the numbers are left unchanged, the labels on the shelves, the notices to users, and the links with other systems also need no modification, which keeps migration cost and confusion to a minimum. Therefore both a and b should use the current ones, and ア is correct.
fields.after: The decisive clues are the two premises set out in the question. First, “the file (table) for managing the lending history will continue to use the one from the current system as-is”; second, “barcodes and RFID are used together during the migration period.” The lending history table records which book was borrowed by whom using the book identification number and the user number. If this table is to keep being used as-is, the keys stored in it, namely both the book identification number in a and the user number in b, must not change from the current numbering scheme. If the numbers were reassigned, the numbers in the past lending history data would no longer match those in new records, the table would have to be rebuilt or converted using a mapping table of numbers, and the aim of “migrating smoothly without halting operations” would collapse. Also, until RFID has been attached to all several hundred thousand books, barcodes and RFID will be mixed, so the same book must be kept in a state where “it has the same identification number whether read by barcode or by RFID”; on this point too, the current numbers must be continued. Therefore both a and b are “use the current one,” and ア is correct. As an incidental benefit, keeping the current numbers also means that the labels on the shelves, the notices to users, and the links with other systems need not change, but this is supplementary; the basis for the judgment is strictly the two premises above.

fields.before: RFID is a mechanism that reads and writes information wirelessly without contact.
